english.html: alty for this crime, although the Emperor makes it capital <sup class="mk" data-key="k">k</sup>, is nevertheless not among the most certain, inasmuch as a capital penalty may refer both to civil death and to natural death <sup class="mk" data-key="l">l</sup>. Wherein I have always been of opinion to leave and commit to the discretion of the Judge the kind of death, who, having weighed the qualities of the persons and balanced all the circumstances, may lighten or aggravate the penalty <sup class="mk" data-key="m">m</sup>: singularly in our France, where cognizance is taken of crimes only extraordinarily; in which case the gravity and lightness of penalties seem to depend entirely upon the Judge <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>.

notes.gloss: The judge fixes the penalty according to the manner of the offence.
One who tries a crime extra ordinem may today pass whatever sentence he wishes, heavier or lighter.

english.html: She had had a preliminary inquiry made into it by authority of the Judge of Rieux; and, claiming the whole to be verified, concluded against the said du Tilh for a double amend: the honourable (amende honorable, public penance), to ask pardon of God, of the King, and of the said de Rols, plaintiff, bareheaded and barefoot, in a shirt, holding a burning torch in his hands, saying that falsely, rashly and treacherously he has deceived, abused, betrayed and circumvented her, in taking the name and substituting the person of Martin Guerre her true husband, of which he repents, and asks her mercy for it; and for the profitable, in two thousand livres, and to costs, damages and interest.

The King's procurator in France is he who prosecutes crimes as regards public vengeance; and a private person with an interest can prosecute only civilly, for his own interest <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, and thus cannot conclude for a capital penalty

notes.citation: Guillaume Benedicti (Guillaume Benoît, 1455–1516), Repetitio on the chapter Raynutius, Decretals X 3.26 (De testamentis), c. 16, on the words mortuo itaque testatore, no. 159
notes.original: Guillaume Benedict. au ch. Raynutius ſur ceſte parole, mortuo itaq; teſt. i. & nõbre 159. de teſta.
notes.gloss: Benoît's vast commentary on the decretal Raynutius, first printed at Lyon in 1522, is the standard French repository on the point; the number 159 is unverified.

uncertain.note: the italic marker k is blotted (a smudge above it); the mark after it, at 5x, is a compact round dot sitting on the baseline with no tail below it, unlike the commas of this line's neighbours ('certeines,'), so it is read as a period although the sentence runs on into 'pourtant'; a worn comma cannot be wholly excluded

abbreviated citation read as 'nesem' with a short round s (could be 'necem', lex si necem); the opening 'l' carries no point, unlike the 'l.' of the other citations; the capital after it is 'P.' (same sort as the 'P.' of note m), not 'D.'

the line-initial siglum is a long ſ followed by a short round s, no point; certainly the Digest siglum usually printed 'ff.', but the sorts do not match the 'ff' ligature of 'effract.' below, so it is transcribed as printed; it sits at the key column but has no marker in the body and is a continuation line of note l
'liberto' is broken across lines and the break is printed as a round dot ('li.' / 'berto.'), not a hyphen; transcribed as printed
first letter read as 'c' ('ch.' = chapitre, cap. Raynutius); at this size it could be read as 'eh.'
the -que sign after 'itaq' is printed as a semicolon shape, not the 3-shaped ꝫ; transcribed ';' per the standing ruling
digits read as 1-5-9 in old-style figures; the 5 is worn
